In traditional <color=#3366CC>colour theory</color>, blue is one of the three <color=#3366CC>primary colours</color> (red, yellow, blue), which can be mixed to form a
decent <color=#3366CC>gamut</color> of colours (although the modern <color=#3366CC>CMY</color> model is able to achieve a much wider gamut). Red and yellow
mixed together form orange, yellow together and blue form green, blue and red form purple, and mixing all three
primary colours together produces a dark brown. From the Renaissance onward, painters used this system to create
their colours (see <color=#3366CC>RYB colour model</color>).
The RYB model was used for colour printing by Jacob Christoph Le Blon as early as 1725. Later, printers discovered
that more accurate colours could be created by using combinations of cyan, magenta, yellow, and black ink, put onto
separate inked plates and then overlaid one at a time onto paper. This method could produce almost all the colours
with reasonable accuracy.
On the <color=#3366CC>HSV colour wheel</color>, the complement of blue is <color=#3366CC>yellow</color>; that is, a colour corresponding to an equal mixture of <color=#3366CC>red</color>
and <color=#3366CC>green</color> light. On a colour wheel based on traditional colour theory (<color=#3366CC>RYB</color>) where blue was considered a primary
colour, its complementary colour is considered to be <color=#3366CC>orange</color>.
LED
In 1993, high-brightness blue LEDs were demonstrated by <color=#3366CC>Shuji Nakamura</color> of Nichia Corporation. In parallel, <color=#3366CC>Isamu</color>
<color=#3366CC>Akasaki</color> and <color=#3366CC>Hiroshi Amano</color> of <color=#3366CC>Nagoya University</color> were working on a new development which revolutionised LED
lighting.
Nakamura was awarded the 2006 Millennium Technology Prize for his invention. Nakamura, Amano and Akasaki were
awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014 for the invention of an efficient blue LED.
Lasers
<color=#3366CC>Lasers</color> emitting in the blue region of the spectrum became widely available to the public in 2010 with the release of
inexpensive high-powered 445–447 nm laser diode technology. Previously the blue wavelengths were accessible only
through DPSS which are comparatively expensive and inefficient, but still widely used by scientists for applications
including optogenetics, <color=#3366CC>Raman spectroscopy</color>, and particle image velocimetry, due to their superior beam quality. Blue

<color=#3366CC>gas lasers</color> are also still commonly used for <color=#3366CC>holography</color>, <color=#3366CC>DNA sequencing</color>, <color=#3366CC>optical pumping</color>, among other scientific and
medical applications.
Shades and variations

Blue is the colour of light between <color=#3366CC>violet</color> and <color=#3366CC>cyan</color> on the <color=#3366CC>visible spectrum</color>. Hues of blue include indigo and <color=#3366CC>ultramarine</color>,
closer to violet; pure blue, without any mixture of other colours; Azure, which is a lighter shade of blue, similar to the
colour of the sky; Cyan, which is midway in the spectrum between blue and <color=#3366CC>green</color>, and the other blue-greens such as
<color=#3366CC>turquoise</color>, <color=#3366CC>teal</color>, and aquamarine.
Blue also varies in shade or tint; darker shades of blue contain black or grey, while lighter tints contain white. Darker

shades of blue include ultramarine, cobalt blue, <color=#3366CC>navy blue</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Prussian blue</color>; while lighter tints include <color=#3366CC>sky blue</color>, <color=#3366CC>azure</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>Egyptian blue</color> (for a more complete list see the List of colours).
As a structural colour
In nature, many blue phenomena arise from <color=#3366CC>structural colouration</color>, the result of interference between reflections from
two or more surfaces of thin films, combined with refraction as light enters and exits such films. The geometry then
determines that at certain angles, the light reflected from both surfaces interferes constructively, while at other angles,
the light interferes destructively. Diverse colours therefore appear despite the absence of colourants.
Colourants
Artificial blues
<color=#3366CC>Egyptian blue</color>, the first artificial pigment, was produced in the third millennium BC in Ancient Egypt. It is produced by
heating pulverised sand, copper, and natron. It was used in tomb paintings and funereal objects to protect the dead in
their afterlife. Prior to the 1700s, blue colourants for artwork were mainly based on lapis lazuli and the related mineral
ultramarine. A breakthrough occurred in 1709 when German druggist and pigment maker Johann Jacob Diesbach
discovered <color=#3366CC>Prussian blue</color>. The new blue arose from experiments involving heating dried blood with iron sulphides and
was initially called Berliner Blau. By 1710 it was being used by the French painter <color=#3366CC>Antoine Watteau</color>, and later his
successor Nicolas Lancret. It became immensely popular for the manufacture of wallpaper, and in the 19th century was
widely used by French impressionist painters. Beginning in the 1820s, Prussian blue was imported into Japan through
the port of <color=#3366CC>Nagasaki</color>. It was called bero-ai, or Berlin blue, and it became popular because it did not fade like traditional
Japanese blue pigment, ai-gami, made from the <color=#3366CC>dayflower</color>. Prussian blue was used by both <color=#3366CC>Hokusai</color>, in his wave
paintings, and <color=#3366CC>Hiroshige</color>.
In 1799 a French chemist, Louis Jacques Thénard, made a synthetic cobalt blue pigment which became immensely
popular with painters.
In 1824 the Societé pour l'Encouragement d'Industrie in France offered a prize for the invention of an artificial
<color=#3366CC>ultramarine</color> which could rival the natural colour made from lapis lazuli. The prize was won in 1826 by a chemist named
Jean Baptiste Guimet, but he refused to reveal the formula of his colour. In 1828, another scientist, Christian Gmelin
then a professor of chemistry in Tübingen, found the process and published his formula. This was the beginning of new
industry to manufacture artificial ultramarine, which eventually almost completely replaced the natural product.
In 1878 the German chemistry and dyeing company Badische Anilin- und Soda-Fabrik (BASF) headed by chemist
Adolf von Baeyer synthesised <color=#3366CC>indigo</color>. This product rapidly replaced natural indigo, wiping out vast farms growing indigo.
It is now the blue of blue jeans. As the pace of <color=#3366CC>organic chemistry</color> accelerated, a succession of synthetic blue dyes were
discovered including Indanthrone blue, which had even greater resistance to fading during washing or in the sun, and
copper phthalocyanine. BASF's work on Indanthrone blue had been a by product of their 17 year research on
synthesizing Indigo and the version "Indigo Pure BASF" which would be commercially produced before Indanthrene
blue would take over popularity.
Dyes for textiles and food
<color=#3366CC>Woad</color> and true indigo were once used but since the early 1900s, all indigo is synthetic. Produced on an industrial scale,
indigo is the blue of blue jeans. Blue dyes are organic compounds, both synthetic and natural.
For food, the triarylmethane dye Brilliant blue FCF is used for candies. The search continues for stable, natural blue
dyes suitable for the food industry.
Various <color=#3366CC>raspberry</color>-flavoured foods are dyed blue. This was done to distinguish it from <color=#3366CC>strawberry</color>, <color=#3366CC>watermelon</color> and
<color=#3366CC>cherry</color>-flavoured foods. The company ICEE used Blue No. 1 for their blue raspberry ICEEs.
Pigments for painting and glass
Blue <color=#3366CC>pigments</color> were once produced from minerals, especially <color=#3366CC>lapis lazuli</color> and its close relative <color=#3366CC>ultramarine</color>. These
minerals were crushed, ground into powder, and then mixed with a quick-drying binding agent, such as egg yolk
(<color=#3366CC>tempera painting</color>); or with a slow-drying oil, such as linseed oil, for <color=#3366CC>oil painting</color>. Two inorganic but synthetic blue
pigments are <color=#3366CC>cerulean blue</color> (primarily cobalt(II) stanate: Co2SnO4) and <color=#3366CC>Prussian blue</color> (milori blue: primarily
Fe7(CN)18). The chromophore in blue <color=#3366CC>glass</color> and glazes is <color=#3366CC>cobalt</color>(II). Diverse cobalt(II) salts such as cobalt carbonate
or cobalt(II) aluminate are mixed with the silica prior to firing. The cobalt occupies sites otherwise filled with silicon.
Inks
Methyl blue is the dominant blue pigment in inks used in pens. <color=#3366CC>Blueprinting</color> involves the production of <color=#3366CC>Prussian blue</color> in
situ.
Inorganic compounds
Certain metal <color=#3366CC>ions</color> characteristically form blue solutions or blue salts. Of some practical importance, <color=#3366CC>cobalt</color> is used to
make the deep blue glazes and glasses. It substitutes for <color=#3366CC>silicon</color> or <color=#3366CC>aluminium</color> ions in these materials. Cobalt is the blue
chromophore in <color=#3366CC>stained glass windows</color>, such as those in Gothic cathedrals and in Chinese <color=#3366CC>porcelain</color> beginning in the
<color=#3366CC>Tang dynasty</color>. <color=#3366CC>Copper(II)</color> (Cu2+) also produces many blue compounds, including the commercial algicide <color=#3366CC>copper(II)</color>
<color=#3366CC>sulphate</color> (CuSO4.5H2O). Similarly, vanadyl salts and solutions are often blue, e.g. vanadyl sulphate.
In nature
Sky and sea
When sunlight passes through the atmosphere, the blue wavelengths are scattered more widely by the oxygen and
nitrogen molecules, and more blue comes to our eyes. This effect is called <color=#3366CC>Rayleigh scattering</color>, after <color=#3366CC>Lord Rayleigh</color> and
confirmed by <color=#3366CC>Albert Einstein</color> in 1911.
The sea is seen as blue for largely the same reason: the water absorbs the longer wavelengths of red and reflects and
scatters the blue, which comes to the eye of the viewer. The deeper the observer goes, the darker the blue becomes.
In the open sea, only about 1% of light penetrates to a depth of 200 metres (see underwater and <color=#3366CC>euphotic depth</color>).
The colour of the sea is also affected by the colour of the sky, reflected by particles in the water; and by <color=#3366CC>algae</color> and plant
life in the water, which can make it look green; or by sediment, which can make it look brown.
The farther away an object is, the more blue it often appears to the eye. For example, mountains in the distance often
appear blue. This is the effect of atmospheric perspective; the farther an object is away from the viewer, the less
contrast there is between the object and its background colour, which is usually blue. In a painting where different parts
of the composition are blue, green and red, the blue will appear to be more distant, and the red closer to the viewer.
The cooler a colour is, the more distant it seems. Blue light is <color=#3366CC>scattered more</color> than other wavelengths by the gases in
the <color=#3366CC>atmosphere</color>, hence our "blue planet".
Minerals
Some of the most desirable gems are blue, including <color=#3366CC>sapphire</color> and <color=#3366CC>tanzanite</color>. Compounds of copper(II) are
characteristically blue and so are many copper-containing minerals. <color=#3366CC>Azurite</color> (Cu3(CO3)2(OH)2), with a deep blue
colour, was once employed in medieval years, but it is unstable pigment, losing its colour especially under dry
conditions. <color=#3366CC>Lapis lazuli</color>, mined in Afghanistan for more than three thousand years, was used for jewellery and
ornaments, and later was crushed and powdered and used as a pigment. The more it was ground, the lighter the blue
colour became. Natural <color=#3366CC>ultramarine</color>, made by grinding lapis lazuli into a fine powder, was the finest available blue
pigment in the Middle Ages and the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>. It was extremely expensive, and in <color=#3366CC>Italian Renaissance</color> art, it was
often reserved for the robes of the <color=#3366CC>Virgin Mary</color>.
Plants and fungi
Intense efforts have focused on blue flowers and the possibility that natural blue colourants could be used as food
dyes. Commonly, blue colours in plants are <color=#3366CC>anthocyanins</color>: "the largest group of water-soluble pigments found
widespread in the plant kingdom". In the few plants that exploit structural colouration, brilliant colours are produced by
structures within cells. The most brilliant blue colouration known in any living tissue is found in the marble berries of
Pollia condensata, where a spiral structure of cellulose fibrils scattering blue light. The fruit of quandong (Santalum
acuminatum) can appear blue owing to the same effect.
Animals
Blue-pigmented animals are relatively rare. Examples of which include butterflies of the genus Nessaea, where blue is
created by pterobilin. Other blue pigments of animal origin include phorcabilin, used by other butterflies in Graphium
and Papilio (specifically P. phorcas and P. weiskei), and sarpedobilin, which is used by Graphium sarpedon.
Blue-pigmented <color=#3366CC>organelles</color>, known as "cyanosomes", exist in the chromatophores of at least two fish species, the
mandarin fish and the picturesque dragonet. More commonly, blueness in animals is a <color=#3366CC>structural colouration</color>; an optical
interference effect induced by organised nanometre-sized scales or fibres. Examples include the plumage of several
birds like the blue jay and indigo bunting, the scales of butterflies like the <color=#3366CC>morpho butterfly</color>, <color=#3366CC>collagen</color> fibres in the skin of
some species of monkey and <color=#3366CC>opossum</color>, and the iridophore cells in some fish and frogs.
Eyes
Blue eyes do not actually contain any blue pigment. <color=#3366CC>Eye colour</color> is determined by two factors: the <color=#3366CC>pigmentation</color> of the
eye's <color=#3366CC>iris</color> and the <color=#3366CC>scattering</color> of light by the turbid medium in the stroma of the iris. In humans, the pigmentation of the iris
varies from light brown to black. The appearance of blue, green, and hazel eyes results from the Tyndall scattering of
light in the stroma, an optical effect similar to what accounts for the blueness of the sky. The irises of the eyes of people
with blue eyes contain less dark <color=#3366CC>melanin</color> than those of people with brown eyes, which means that they absorb less
short-wavelength blue light, which is instead reflected out to the viewer. Eye colour also varies depending on the
lighting conditions, especially for lighter-coloured eyes.
Blue eyes are most common in Ireland, the <color=#3366CC>Baltic Sea</color> area and <color=#3366CC>Northern Europe</color>, and are also found in <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Central</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Southern Europe</color>. Blue eyes are also found in parts of <color=#3366CC>Western Asia</color>, most notably in <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Iraq</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>. In <color=#3366CC>Estonia</color>, 99% of people have blue eyes. In <color=#3366CC>Denmark</color> in 1978, only 8% of the population had brown
eyes, though through immigration, today that number is about 11%. In <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, about 75% have blue eyes.
In the United States, as of 2006, 1 out of every 6 people, or 16.6% of the total population, and 22.3% of the white
population, have blue eyes, compared with about half of Americans born in 1900, and a third of Americans born in
1950. Blue eyes are becoming less common among American children. In the US, males are 3–5% more likely to have
blue eyes than females.
History
In the ancient world
As early as the 7th millennium BC, lapis lazuli was mined in the Sar-i Sang mines, in Shortugai, and in other mines in
<color=#3366CC>Badakhshan</color> province in northeast <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>.
Lapis lazuli artefacts, dated to 7570 BC, have been found at Bhirrana, which is the oldest site of <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley</color>
<color=#3366CC>civilisation</color>. Lapis was highly valued by the Indus Valley Civilisation (7570–1900 BC). Lapis beads have been found at

<color=#3366CC>Neolithic</color> burials in Mehrgarh, the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color>, and as far away as <color=#3366CC>Mauritania</color>. It was used in the <color=#3366CC>funeral mask of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Tutankhamun</color> (1341–1323 BC).
A term for Blue was relatively rare in many forms of ancient art and decoration, and even in ancient literature. The
Ancient Greek poets described the sea as green, brown or "the colour of wine". The colour is mentioned several times
in the <color=#3366CC>Hebrew Bible</color> as 'tekhelet'. Reds, blacks, browns, and ochres are found in <color=#3366CC>cave paintings</color> from the Upper
<color=#3366CC>Paleolithic</color> period, but not blue. Blue was also not used for dyeing fabric until long after red, ochre, pink, and purple.
This is probably due to the perennial difficulty of making blue dyes and pigments. On the other hand, the rarity of blue
pigment made it even more valuable.
The earliest known blue dyes were made from plants – <color=#3366CC>woad</color> in Europe, <color=#3366CC>indigo</color> in Asia and Africa, while blue pigments
were made from minerals, usually either <color=#3366CC>lapis lazuli</color> or <color=#3366CC>azurite</color>, and required more. Blue glazes posed still another
challenge since the early blue dyes and pigments were not thermally robust. In c. 2500 BC, the blue glaze <color=#3366CC>Egyptian</color>
<color=#3366CC>blue</color> was introduced for ceramics, as well as many other objects. The Greeks imported indigo dye from India, calling it
indikon, and they painted with Egyptian blue. Blue was not one of the four primary colours for Greek painting described
by <color=#3366CC>Pliny the Elder</color> (red, yellow, black, and white). For the Romans, blue was the colour of mourning, as well as the
colour of barbarians. The Celts and Germans reportedly dyed their faces blue to frighten their enemies, and tinted their
hair blue when they grew old. The Romans made extensive use of indigo and Egyptian blue pigment, as evidenced, in
part, by frescos in <color=#3366CC>Pompeii</color>. The Romans had many words for varieties of blue, including caeruleus, caesius, glaucus,
cyaneus, lividus, venetus, aerius, and ferreus, but two words, both of foreign origin, became the most enduring; blavus,
from the Germanic word blau, which eventually became bleu or blue; and azureus, from the Arabic word lazaward,
which became azure.
Blue was widely used in the decoration of churches in the Byzantine Empire. By contrast, in the Islamic world, blue was
of secondary to green, believed to be the favourite colour of the <color=#3366CC>Prophet Mohammed</color>. At certain times in <color=#3366CC>Moorish Spain</color>
and other parts of the Islamic world, blue was the colour worn by Christians and Jews, because only Muslims were
allowed to wear white and green.
In the Middle Ages
In the art and life of Europe during the early <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>, blue played a minor role. This changed dramatically between
1130 and 1140 in Paris, when the <color=#3366CC>Abbe Suger</color> rebuilt the <color=#3366CC>Saint Denis Basilica</color>. Suger considered that light was the
visible manifestation of the Holy Spirit. He installed <color=#3366CC>stained glass</color> windows coloured with <color=#3366CC>cobalt</color>, which, combined with
the light from the red glass, filled the church with a bluish violet light. The church became the marvel of the <color=#3366CC>Christian</color>
<color=#3366CC>world</color>, and the colour became known as the "bleu de Saint-Denis". In the years that followed even more elegant blue
stained glass windows were installed in other churches, including at <color=#3366CC>Chartres Cathedral</color> and Sainte-Chapelle in Paris.
In the 12th century the Roman Catholic Church dictated that painters in Italy (and the rest of Europe consequently) to
paint the Virgin Mary with blue, which became associated with holiness, humility and virtue. In medieval paintings, blue
was used to attract the attention of the viewer to the Virgin Mary. Paintings of the mythical <color=#3366CC>King Arthur</color> began to show
him dressed in blue. The coat of arms of the kings of France became an azure or light blue shield, sprinkled with
golden <color=#3366CC>fleur-de-lis</color> or lilies. Blue had come from obscurity to become the royal colour.
Renaissance through 18th century
Blue came into wider use beginning in the Renaissance, when artists began to paint the world with perspective, depth,
shadows, and light from a single source. In Renaissance paintings, artists tried to create harmonies between blue and
red, lightening the blue with lead white paint and adding shadows and highlights. <color=#3366CC>Raphael</color> was a master of this
technique, carefully balancing the reds and the blues so no one colour dominated the picture.
<color=#3366CC>Ultramarine</color> was the most prestigious blue of the Renaissance, being more expensive than gold. Wealthy art patrons
commissioned works with the most expensive blues possible. In 1616 Richard Sackville commissioned a portrait of
himself by Isaac Oliver with three different blues, including ultramarine pigment for his stockings.
An industry for the manufacture of fine blue and white pottery began in the 14th century in <color=#3366CC>Jingdezhen</color>, China, using
white Chinese porcelain decorated with patterns of cobalt blue, imported from Persia. It was first made for the family of
the Emperor of China, then was exported around the world, with designs for export adapted to European subjects and
tastes. The Chinese blue style was also adapted by Dutch craftsmen in Delft and English craftsmen in <color=#3366CC>Staffordshire</color> in
the 17th-18th centuries. in the 18th century, blue and white porcelains were produced by <color=#3366CC>Josiah Wedgwood</color> and other
British craftsmen.
19th-20th century
The early 19th century saw the ancestor of the modern blue business suit, created by <color=#3366CC>Beau Brummell</color> (1776–1840),
who set fashion at the London Court. It also saw the invention of <color=#3366CC>blue jeans</color>, a highly popular form of workers's
costume, invented in 1853 by <color=#3366CC>Jacob W. Davis</color> who used metal rivets to strengthen blue <color=#3366CC>denim</color> work clothing in the
California gold fields. The invention was funded by San Francisco entrepreneur <color=#3366CC>Levi Strauss</color>, and spread around the
world.
Recognising the emotional power of blue, many artists made it the central element of paintings in the 19th and 20th
centuries. They included Pablo Picasso, Pavel Kuznetsov and the Blue Rose art group, and <color=#3366CC>Kandinsky</color> and <color=#3366CC>Der Blaue</color>
<color=#3366CC>Reiter</color> (The Blue Rider) school. <color=#3366CC>Henri Matisse</color> expressed deep emotions with blue, "A certain blue penetrates your
soul." In the second half of the 20th century, painters of the <color=#3366CC>abstract expressionist</color> movement use blues to inspire ideas
and emotions. Painter <color=#3366CC>Mark Rothko</color> observed that colour was "only an instrument;" his interest was "in expressing
human emotions tragedy, ecstasy, doom, and so on".
In society and culture
Uniforms
In the 17th century. The Prince-Elector of Brandenburg, <color=#3366CC>Frederick William I of Prussia</color>, chose <color=#3366CC>Prussian blue</color> as the new
colour of Prussian military uniforms, because it was made with <color=#3366CC>Woad</color>, a local crop, rather than <color=#3366CC>Indigo</color>, which was
produced by the colonies of Brandenburg's rival, England. It was worn by the German army until World War I, with the
exception of the soldiers of Bavaria, who wore sky-blue.
In 1748, the <color=#3366CC>Royal Navy</color> adopted a dark shade of blue for the uniform of officers. It was first known as marine blue, now
known as <color=#3366CC>navy blue</color>. The militia organised by <color=#3366CC>George Washington</color> selected blue and buff, the colours of the British
Whig Party. Blue continued to be the colour of the field uniform of the US Army until 1902, and is still the colour of the
dress uniform.
In the 19th century, police in the United Kingdom, including the Metropolitan Police and the City of London Police also
adopted a navy blue uniform. Similar traditions were embraced in France and Austria. It was also adopted at about the
same time for the uniforms of the officers of the New York City Police Department.
Gender
Blue is used to represent <color=#3366CC>males</color>. Beginning as a trend the mid-19th century and applying primarily to clothing, gendered
associations with blue became more widespread from the 1950s. The colour became associated with males after <color=#3366CC>World</color>
<color=#3366CC>War II</color>.
Religion
• Blue in Judaism: In the <color=#3366CC>Torah</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Israelites</color> were commanded to put fringes, tzitzit, on the corners of their
garments, and to weave within these fringes a "twisted thread of blue (tekhelet)". In ancient days, this blue thread
was made from a dye extracted from a Mediterranean snail called the hilazon. The dye of the hilazon is said to
come from either the snail Hexaplex trunculus, the cuttlefish, or the sea worm Bonellia viridis. <color=#3366CC>Maimonides</color> claimed
that this blue was the colour of "the clear noonday sky"; <color=#3366CC>Rashi</color>, the colour of the evening sky. According to several
rabbinic sages, blue is the colour of God's Glory. Staring at this colour aids in mediation, bringing us a glimpse of
the "pavement of sapphire, like the very sky for purity", which is a likeness of the Throne of God. (The <color=#3366CC>Hebrew</color> word
for glory) Many items in the Mishkan, the portable sanctuary in the wilderness, such as the <color=#3366CC>menorah</color>, many of the
vessels, and the <color=#3366CC>Ark of the Covenant</color>, were covered with blue cloth when transported from place to place.
• Blue in <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>: Blue is particularly associated with the <color=#3366CC>Virgin Mary</color>. This was the result of a decree of <color=#3366CC>Pope</color>
<color=#3366CC>Gregory I</color> (540–601) who ordered that all religious paintings should tell a story which was clearly comprehensible to
all viewers, and that figures should be easily recognisable, especially that of the figure of Mary. If she was alone in
the image, her costume was usually painted with the finest blue, <color=#3366CC>ultramarine</color>. If she was with Christ, her costume
was usually painted with a less expensive pigment, to avoid outshining him.
• Blue in <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>: Many of the gods are depicted as having blue-coloured skin, particularly those associated with
<color=#3366CC>Vishnu</color>, who is said to be the preserver of the world, and thus intimately connected to water. <color=#3366CC>Krishna</color> and <color=#3366CC>Rama</color>,
Vishnu's avatars, are usually depicted with blue skin. <color=#3366CC>Shiva</color>, the destroyer deity, is also depicted in a light-blue hue,
and is called Nīlakantha, or blue-throated, for having swallowed poison to save the universe during the Samudra
Manthana, the churning of the ocean of milk. Blue is used to symbolically represent the fifth, and the throat, <color=#3366CC>chakra</color>
(Vishuddha).
• Blue in <color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color>: The Akali Nihangs warriors wear all-blue attire. <color=#3366CC>Guru Gobind Singh</color> also has a blue roan <color=#3366CC>horse</color>.
The Sikh Rehat Maryada states that the Nishan Sahib hoisted outside every <color=#3366CC>Gurudwara</color> should be <color=#3366CC>xanthic</color> (Basanti
in <color=#3366CC>Punjabi</color>) or greyish blue (modern day <color=#3366CC>navy blue</color>) (Surmaaee in <color=#3366CC>Punjabi</color>) colour.
Sports
In sports, blue is widely represented in uniforms in part because the majority of national teams wear the colours of their
national flag. For example, the national men's football team of France are known as Les Bleus (the Blues). Similarly,
<color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, and Uruguay wear blue shirts. The Asian Football Confederation and the Oceania Football
Confederation use blue text on their logos. Blue is well represented in <color=#3366CC>baseball</color> (Blue Jays), <color=#3366CC>basketball</color>, and <color=#3366CC>American</color>

<color=#3366CC>football</color>, and <color=#3366CC>ice hockey</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Indian national cricket team</color> wears blue uniform during <color=#3366CC>One day international</color> matches, as
such the team is also referred to as "Men in Blue".
Politics
Unlike red or green, blue was not strongly associated with any particular country, religion or political movement. As the
colour of harmony, it was chosen as the colour for the flags of the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color>, the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>, and <color=#3366CC>NATO</color>. In
politics, blue is often used as the colour of conservative parties, contrasting with the red associated with left-wing
parties. Some conservative parties that use the colour blue include the <color=#3366CC>Conservative Party (UK)</color>, Conservative Party of
Canada, Liberal Party of Australia, Liberal Party of Brazil, and <color=#3366CC>Likud</color> of Israel. However, in some countries, blue is not
associated main conservative party. In the United States, the liberal <color=#3366CC>Democratic Party</color> is associated with blue, while the
conservative <color=#3366CC>Republican Party</color> is associated with red. US states which have been won by the Democratic Party in four
consecutive presidential elections are termed "blue states", while those that have been won by the Republican Party
are termed "red states". <color=#3366CC>South Korea</color> also uses this colour model, with the Democratic Party on the left using blue and
the People Power Party on the right using red.
